title: What Have We Learned About Better Explanations?
author: Science of Explanation
summary: Marking six months and 24 posts, this digest distills the newsletter's central research threads on how the mind processes explanations, using an AI notebook tool to summarize the author's own back catalog with edits and framing added by the author. It organizes findings under headings like preparation and audience strategy, and earning initial attention, covering ideas such as treating explanation as a 'prediction problem,' each person's unique 'sensory bubble,' the 'curse of knowledge,' and the need to lead with relevance to capture attention before anything else can land. The piece is candid about its own method, disclosing that an AI tool (Gemini Notebook) produced the bullet points from the author's prior writing. It closes by previewing the next phase of the project: extending the framework toward reasoning, mental models, and neurodiversity in how people process explanations.
points: Treat explanation as a 'prediction problem': since knowledge can't be transferred directly, success depends on accurately predicting what representation will work for a given audience.
Guard against the 'curse of knowledge' — the more you know, the harder it becomes to imagine not knowing, so make the invisible visible for your audience rather than assuming shared context.
Recognize everyone's unique 'sensory bubble': people perceive reality differently based on biology and experience, so successful explainers build a shared baseline first.
Lead with relevance in the first few sentences to earn attention before anything else in an explanation can succeed.
Treat six months of accumulated research as a 'gauntlet of the mind' framework tracing the path an idea takes from first exposure to lasting memory.
quotes: This newsletter is based on a big idea: We can become better communicators by understanding the mechanics of the mind.
People don’t share knowledge directly. Everything we communicate is a representation of what we know.
Everyone perceives a unique version of reality based on their biology and experience.
The more you know, the harder it is to imagine not knowing. Don’t assume your audience shares your context; make the invisible visible for them.
Lead with relevance: In your first few sentences, signal why the information is urgent or relevant to the audience’s goals, threats, or emotions.
